name: Ceramide AP

lead: Ceramides are waxy lipids that, with cholesterol and fatty acids, fill the gaps between skin cells in the outer layer, limiting water loss. Ceramide AP is one of the epidermal ceramide classes (a phytoceramide) used in skincare.
Moisturisers add ceramides to support the barrier, helping dry or irritated skin look and feel smoother.

paras: It is applied as part of leave-on creams and lotions, often together with cholesterol and fatty acids, as part of a daily moisturising routine.
Ceramide moisturisers are generally well tolerated; as with any cosmetic, individual sensitivities to other ingredients can occur.

angle.text: A barrier-supporting moisturiser helps skin stay hydrated and calm, which affects how smooth and even it looks.

lead: Ceramides are lipids made of sphingosine and a fatty acid. In the skin's outermost layer, the stratum corneum, they sit between dead cells in a "bricks and mortar" arrangement and, with cholesterol and free fatty acids, form a water-resistant barrier.[1]

Ceramide AP is one of the epidermal ceramide classes, grouped as a phytoceramide with NP.[1] Skincare uses ceramides in creams, soaps, shampoos and sunscreens, and they are added to some eczema products.[1]
Barrier lipid levels can fall with dry or polluted air, harsh sulfates, heat, UV and aging.[1] Replenishing them is the basis for ceramide moisturisers.

paras: By weight the barrier lipid matrix is roughly 50% ceramides, 25% cholesterol and 15% free fatty acids.[1] In psoriasis some ceramide classes rise while others fall, which may weaken the barrier.[1]

No studies found on Ceramide AP alone in appearance outcomes. A 2016 pilot study evaluated an over-the-counter eczema product combining botanical agents,[2] and lab studies have built stratum corneum lipid models for research.[3]
